theme: The Day of Atonement, the center of the entire system
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 16:1-34. This is the most important chapter in the book. Read it slowly, and picture the high priest going through the veil with blood. Then notice the two goats and what happens to each.
settingTheScene: The Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, is the one day of the year when the high priest enters the Most Holy Place. The chapter begins with a reminder of the death of Nadab and Abihu (16:1), because the sanctuary is dangerous. Over the year, the tabernacle has been defiled by the sins of the people, and on this one day it is cleansed, and the sins of the nation are dealt with. It is the center of the whole system, and everything else in Leviticus is built around it.
observation: Aaron may not come “at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil” or he will die (16:2).
He bathes, puts on holy linen garments, and offers a bull for his own sin first (16:3-4, 11).
He takes a censer of burning coals and incense into the Most Holy Place, “so that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat” (16:12-13).
He sprinkles the blood of the bull and the goat on the mercy seat and before it (16:14-15).
“Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins” (16:16).
Two goats are chosen. One is the LORD’s, killed as a sin offering. The other is the scapegoat (16:7-10).
Aaron lays both hands on the live goat, confesses “all the iniquities of the people of Israel,” and sends it into the wilderness (16:21-22).

“For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins” (16:30). The day is to be a Sabbath of solemn rest, and a day of fasting, for all time (16:29-31).
interpretation:
This chapter gathers up everything you have read in Leviticus so far. There are four parts, and each has a lesson.

First, there is the high priest’s preparation. He cannot simply walk into God’s presence. He must bathe, change his clothes, and offer a bull for his own sin. Even the mediator needs a mediator. The priest is a sinner, and his own sin has to be covered before he can cover anyone else’s. There is a built-in sense that this system is incomplete.

Second, there is the entry into the Most Holy Place. Once a year, one man goes behind the veil, with a cloud of incense to shield him, and sprinkles blood on the mercy seat. This is the place where the tablets of the law lay, the testimony against Israel’s sin. The blood goes between the law and the presence of God. The place that would condemn is covered by blood. This is atonement at its most vivid.

Third, there is the cleansing of the sanctuary. The tabernacle itself is purified because of the people’s sin. Sin pollutes even the place where God lives, and it must be cleansed or God’s presence cannot remain. This is an important idea. Sin has real effects on the world.

Fourth, there are the two goats. One dies, and its blood is used to cover sin. The other lives, and the sins of the people are placed on its head. It is sent away into the wilderness, to a remote and uninhabited place (16:22). Together, the two goats show two sides of atonement: sin is paid for, and sin is carried away. The people see their sin removed, and they know that it is gone.

Yet the sacrifice has to be repeated every year. Hebrews will say that this repetition is itself the proof that the blood of animals cannot finally take away sin. The Day of Atonement points beyond itself to a greater sacrifice, one that does not need to be offered again.
connection: Hebrews 9 and 10 interpret this chapter in detail. Christ entered “once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The veil was torn in two at his death (Matthew 27:51). He is the sacrifice and the high priest. Romans 3:25 says that God put him forward “as a propitiation by his blood.” John the Baptist says, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29), and Isaiah 53:6 says that “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
application:
Read Hebrews 9:11-14 and 10:19-22 today. Notice the contrast with Leviticus 16, and thank God for the finished work of Christ.

Picture the scapegoat going into the wilderness with your sins. Ask God to help you believe that they are truly gone.

Because the sacrifice is finished, you can come near with confidence. Spend a few minutes in unhurried prayer.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for fulfilling the Day of Atonement once for all.
Ask for a true heart and full assurance as you draw near.
Tell God what it means to you that your sins have been carried away.
